Q: What sorting methods would I use for the following problem? A:

It is important to realize that "Which algorithm performs best?" and "Which algorithm should I use?" are two distinct question.

Sorting algorithms are subject of active research. When designing sorting algorithms it is important to consider the large range of possible different inputs. Existance of duplicates and how much the input is sorted / unsorted and other factors can have huge impact on how a sorting algorithm performs. When a sorting algorithm is evaluated it is evaluated based on how it performs on any possible input.

On the other hand, when you are looking for the best algorithm for a specific problem then your input is not arbitrary. Often you also don't care about asymptotic complexity when you know the size of the input. For given input the actual runtime of a O(N^2) algorithm can be less than that of a O(N logN) algorithm. With a specific problem at hand you don't care if an algorithm performs better or worse on average when it does good enough for your specific case. Because of that, the only way to know which sorting algorithm performs best for your specific case is to profile and measure.

However, don't aim for the most performant unless you have to. Very rarely you have to. In a realistic scenario there are constraints that you have to meet. You can try really any algorithm and if it is fast enough you are done. std::sort is not using the optimal algorithm for all possible input, but typically it is good enough. Only if you cannot achieve the goal with std::sort you have to look elsewhere.

Q: Microsoft Entra ID login shows “Access Denied – You do not have permission to sign in” with NextAuth v5 (Auth.js) and Next.js 15 A:

Hit the same thing in our Next.js + NextAuth v5 + Entra ID setup. Two things to check.

Add a console.log inside your signIn callback and print account, profile, user. If account comes through undefined, or the provider name is not exactly "microsoft-entra-id", your else branch fires and you get the access denied page.

Second, your NEXTAUTH_MICROSOFT_ENTRA_ID_ISSUER. With Entra you need a full issuer URL including the tenant id, like https://login.microsoftonline.com/your-tenant-id/v2.0. If it is empty or just the host, token validation fails silently and NextAuth shows the same access denied screen.

What does the debug output look like in your terminal? You have debug true so it should print the actual reason.

Q: Pointer arithmetic within array using a pointer to objects created placement-new A:

There are a couple of questions at hand here.

1. Is it guaranteed that a BlockType will be suitably aligned for a DataType?

In C++11, an allocation function ([basic.stc.dynamic.allocation]) was only required to be aligned enough for an object with an alignment requirement less than or equal to that of std::max_align_t.

The pointer returned shall be suitably aligned so that it can be converted to a pointer of any complete object type with a fundamental alignment requirement ([basic.align]) and then used to access the object or array in the storage allocated (until the storage is explicitly deallocated by a call to a corresponding deallocation function).

However, C++17 added a new overload for operator new, so that the overload set detects whether the alignment of the type is greater than __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, in which case it calls the function that can allocate storage suitably aligned for an object of such a type ([expr.new]).

2. Is it valid to index into the pointer returned by .data()?

As has been noted in previous answers, a[b] is equivalent to *(a + b). Per [expr.add]:

When an expression J that has integral type is added to or subtracted from an expression P of pointer type, the result has the type of P.

[...] if P points to a (possibly-hypothetical) array element 𝑖 of an array object x with 𝑛 elements ([dcl.array]),59 the expressions P + J and J + P (where J has the value 𝑗) point to the (possibly-hypothetical) array element 𝑖+𝑗 of x if 0 ≤ 𝑖+𝑗 ≤ 𝑛 and the expression P - J points to the (possibly-hypothetical) array element 𝑖−𝑗 of x if 0 ≤ 𝑖−𝑗 ≤ 𝑛.

The trouble arises when we consider whether the pointer returned from calling .data() actually points to an element of an array of DataTypes. The method implementation simply performs a reinterpret_cast conversion on data_ptr to a DataType*, the result of which would only point to an element of an array of DataTypes if data_ptr were already pointing to such an element, which it does not immediately after .allocate is called.

Looking at the implementation of .allocate more closely, it allocates an array of BlockTypes, and then reuses the storage of that array by placement-new–ing DataTypes in the buffer. Once the storage is reused, the lifetime of the array ends, even though the storage is still allocated; this means that the returned ptr does not point to any BlockType or DataType object, only allocated memory where an object lives ([basic.life]).

After the lifetime of an object has ended and before the storage which the object occupied is reused or released, if a new object is created at the storage location which the original object occupied and the original object was transparently replaceable by the new object, a pointer that pointed to the original object, a reference that referred to the original object, or the name of the original object will automatically refer to the new object and, once the lifetime of the new object has started, can be used to manipulate the new object.

[Note 6: If these conditions are not met, a pointer to the new object can be obtained from a pointer that represents the address of its storage by calling std​::​launder ([ptr.launder]). — end note]

So in C++17, the solution is simple.

T* data() {
    return std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(data_ptr));
}

Note that the existing class design means that all functions needing a reference to the array and not simply its storage have to call .data(). Whether this warrants a refactor is up to you.

Q: how to make a adjacency matrix in C++ for a surface A:

Adjacency of points on a sphere is quite different from adjacency of a planar net, because the points may wrap
around the sphere, and there is no unique cut through the edges on the sphere that can be developped into a planar net.
(I.e, wrapping a planar net around a sphere may mean that sphere points are very close which are not close in the planar representation.)
A standard way to proceed is to find a Delaunay triangulation of the points on the sphere (for example with the http://www.qhull.org/ construction) and to define adjacency such that points are adjacent if they have a connecting edge in the Delaunay net.
